uncited: Object-order rendering is a family of volume rendering techniques that compute the image by iterating over the volumetric data (the "objects") and projecting their contributions onto the 2D image plane [S5, unofficial].

It solves the problem of efficiently mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D screen by leveraging standard graphics hardware rasterization pipelines, contrasting with image-order methods (like ray casting) that iterate over pixels and trace rays into the volume [S5, unofficial].
It is distinguished from its siblings by its feed-forward nature: information flows from the volume to the screen, whereas image-order methods query the volume from the screen [S5, unofficial].
The object-order family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized [S1, S3, S4, unofficial].
**Primitive Representation:** The volume is decomposed into primitives.
These may be explicit geometric shapes (cubes, cells, splats) or implicit functions sampled via texture hardware [S1, S3, S4, unofficial].
**Transformation:** Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp) [S2, S3, S4, unofficial].
**Rasterization:** The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane.
This step leverages hardware-accelerated scan-conversion, depth testing, and blending [S1, S2, S3, S4, unofficial].
**Compositing:** Contributions are accumulated to form the final image.
This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly [S1, S2, S3, S7, book].
**Hardware Acceleration:** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity [S1, S2, S3, book].
Object-order rendering emerged as a response to the computational cost of early image-order ray casting methods, aiming to leverage the growing power of graphics hardware.
The term "object-order" highlights the direction of data flow: from the volume (object) to the image (screen) [S5, unofficial].
Early implementations focused on rasterizing explicit geometry (voxels as cubes) or using texture mapping for slicing [S1, S3, book].
The family has evolved to include sophisticated techniques like splatting and shear-warp, which balance quality and performance [S2, S7, book].
